---
title: "Research"
---

I study **how emotion regulation is constructed**: not as a skill that sits
inside a child, but as something assembled across biology, relationships, and
context, and across timescales from seconds to years.

Three things follow, and they organise the work below. Regulation is
**coordinated**, using many strategies across many domains rather than one
strategy in one domain. It is **co-regulated**, happening between people and not
only inside the child. And **context is foreground**, not background.

## Biopsychosocial self-regulation

Regulation is not a trait and not a single strategy. Within one frustrating
episode a preschooler will try several things in sequence, distracting, seeking
help, then venting, while their parasympathetic activity shifts underneath.
Measuring regulation *statically*, as a questionnaire score or a single observed
strategy, has held the field back.

My work measures it as it unfolds: **polyregulation**, how strategies combine,
and **temporal variation in respiratory sinus arrhythmia** across an episode. I
follow the same question across **preschool, middle childhood, and
adolescence**, because what counts as skilled regulation changes with age even
when the underlying process does not.

::: {.diagram}

## Stress, adaptation, and resilience

Social stressors affect health through pathways that are visible in daily life
before they are visible in disease. The stressors themselves sit at different
levels: **chronic context** such as socioeconomic risk operates on a different
timescale from **daily events** such as a discriminatory encounter or an exam.

Emotion regulation and physiological regulation are **parallel systems**, not a
sequence. Affect dynamics and cardiac regulation are two readings of the same
adaptive process, coupled to each other but neither reducible to the other.

**Resilience appears twice.** It moderates how a stressor translates into a
regulatory signature, and it is itself an outcome of that process, which is why
it cannot be treated as a fixed trait.

## Family and intergenerational dynamics

**Regulation is learned from interactions.** In Chinese three-generation
households it is co-performed: grandmother, mother, and child regulate together,
sometimes in physiological lockstep. The relationship and the physiology are not
separate stories. How securely a child is attached to each caregiver is part of
what determines whether their bodies couple during a difficult moment, and that
coupling is the mechanism through which regulation transfers.

## Peer relations and friendship development

My dissertation moves this question into the peer world, in two studies.
**Study 1** asks whether the *structure* of an adolescent's friendships, how
diverse their cliques are, how stable, how overlapping, predicts physiological
wear-and-tear and mental health. **Study 2** asks whether friends who cope
similarly amplify or buffer each other, and whether it is similarity in the
*form* of coping or in its *function* that matters.
